questions.question: Which mechanism best explains the chronic itch-scratch cycle in atopic dermatitis?
choices: Barrier dysfunction and inflammation cause itch, scratching causes more barrier injury and inflammation
A bacterial infection is always present in all eczema
Melanocytes stop producing pigment and create itch
Reduced blood flow is the usual primary cause
questions.explanation: Atopic dermatitis involves barrier dysfunction and immune inflammation. Dryness and inflammation cause itch; scratching damages skin further, which perpetuates the cycle and can increase infection risk.

questions.question: Which new finding in a patient with known atopic dermatitis most strongly requires urgent evaluation rather than a routine refill?
choices: Chronic dry itchy flexural patches without systemic symptoms
Abrupt painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions with fever
Mild xerosis after a hot shower
Stable lichenification after years of scratching
questions.explanation: Painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions with fever in eczema raise concern for eczema herpeticum, which needs urgent assessment and should not be treated as an ordinary flare.

questions.question: A rash has sharply defined borders matching the area of a new adhesive product and is more itchy than painful. What diagnosis should be high in the differential?
choices: Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis
Necrotizing soft-tissue infection
Acute ischemic limb
Diabetic retinopathy
questions.explanation: A distribution that maps to a new exposure is a key clue for contact dermatitis. Exposure timing, morphology, and symptoms should be used to confirm or challenge the suspected diagnosis.

questions.question: Why should an FNP be cautious about escalating topical corticosteroids for an annular scaly lesion that enlarges despite treatment?
choices: Topical steroids always cure dermatophyte infection
The lesion may be tinea or another mimic, and steroid use can alter its appearance
All annular lesions are psoriasis
Corticosteroids are contraindicated on every body site
questions.explanation: An enlarging annular scaly lesion may represent dermatophyte infection. Steroids can reduce visible inflammation while allowing fungal disease to persist or become less typical, so the diagnosis should be reconsidered.

questions.question: Which assessment element best reflects FNP-level atopic dermatitis severity?
choices: Only the number of prescriptions previously tried
Sleep disruption, work or school effect, itch, infection signs, site, extent, and treatment access
Whether the rash is visible in a single photo
The patient’s age alone
questions.explanation: Atopic dermatitis severity includes symptoms, sleep, function, psychological burden, infection, distribution, objective skin findings, response to treatment, and practical barriers—not just the visible area.

questions.question: Which foundational barrier-care instruction is most appropriate for many patients with atopic dermatitis?
choices: Use multiple fragranced products to identify the strongest scent
Take very hot prolonged showers and scrub affected skin
Use brief lukewarm bathing, gentle cleansing, and a bland emollient promptly after drying
Avoid all bathing indefinitely
questions.explanation: Brief lukewarm bathing, gentle cleansing, and prompt application of a bland emollient can support barrier repair. Hot water, harsh scrubbing, and fragrance commonly worsen irritation.

questions.question: Which situation most clearly warrants reassessing the diagnosis or arranging dermatology referral?
choices: A patient has a compatible flare that improves with a clear plan
An eruption is atypical, repeatedly fails appropriate treatment, or treatment worsens it
The patient asks how much moisturizer to use
A patient reports mild stable itch that does not affect function
questions.explanation: Diagnostic uncertainty, atypical morphology, recurrent infection, severe disease, special-site involvement, and treatment failure are reasons to reconsider the diagnosis and involve dermatology rather than endlessly escalating empiric therapy.

questions.question: What is the safest interpretation of a positive surface swab from a chronic eczematous patch without clinical infection?
choices: It proves systemic antibiotics are needed
It replaces examination for warmth, pain, purulence, systemic symptoms, and progression
It may reflect colonization and should not alone determine antimicrobial treatment
It excludes eczema herpeticum
questions.explanation: Skin can be colonized without clinical infection. Antimicrobial decisions should follow a clinical assessment for infection, not a surface result alone.

questions.question: Which feature most strongly suggests a potentially serious soft-tissue infection rather than uncomplicated eczema?
choices: Stable chronic pruritus
Rapidly progressive pain, bullae, dusky skin, systemic toxicity, or crepitus
Mild dryness after handwashing
Localized post-inflammatory pigment change
questions.explanation: Rapid progression, disproportionate pain, bullae, dusky or necrotic skin, systemic toxicity, or crepitus can indicate deep or necrotizing infection and requires emergency evaluation.

questions.question: Why is follow-up essential after starting an atopic dermatitis plan?
choices: It only confirms that a prescription was sent
It assesses response, treatment technique, access, adverse effects, infection, function, and whether the diagnosis still fits
Atopic dermatitis always resolves after one visit
It eliminates the need for return precautions
questions.explanation: Follow-up confirms whether the plan is feasible and effective, detects infection or adverse effects, and prompts diagnostic reconsideration or referral when response is not as expected.
